title: The Comet: The Jet That Kept Breaking Apart

chapters.name: Intro
sentences: In nineteen fifty-two, one airplane made every other airliner in the world look old.
It flew twice as high as the others. It was much faster. And inside, it was so smooth that passengers could stand a coin on its edge.
It was called the Comet. It was the first jet airliner in the world.
Then, one after another, Comets began to break apart in the sky.
Nobody knew why. To find the answer, engineers had to invent a new way to investigate a crash.
This is the story of the jet that kept breaking apart, and how it made every flight you take today safer.

chapters.name: A New Kind of Plane
sentences: After the Second World War, airliners still used propellers. They were slow and loud, and they shook for the whole flight.
They also flew low, right through the clouds and the bad weather.
A British company called de Havilland wanted something completely different. A passenger plane with jet engines.
The Comet had four jet engines hidden inside its wings. Its shape was clean and smooth, like nothing else at any airport.
On the twenty-seventh of July, nineteen forty-nine, it flew for the first time.
Britain was now years ahead of every other country.

chapters.name: The First Jet Airline
sentences: On the second of May, nineteen fifty-two, the first jet airline service in history took off from London, heading for Johannesburg.
The Comet cruised at about four hundred and ninety miles per hour. The best propeller airliners flew at around three hundred and fifteen.
It also flew much higher, at up to forty-two thousand feet. That is above most of the weather.
For the passengers, it felt like the future. The flight was quiet and smooth, far above the clouds, with the sky almost black overhead.
But flying that high creates a problem. The air up there is far too thin to breathe.
So the cabin has to be pumped full of air, like a balloon. The thin metal skin of the plane holds that pressure in.
On every flight, the cabin is filled, and then emptied again. The metal stretches a little, and relaxes. Again, and again, and again.
In nineteen fifty-two, nobody fully understood what that does to metal over time.

chapters.name: The First Warning
sentences: Exactly one year after that first service, on the second of May, nineteen fifty-three, a Comet took off from Calcutta in India.
A few minutes later, it flew into a violent thunderstorm. The plane broke apart in the air.
All forty-three people on board were killed.
Investigators blamed the storm. The weather that night was extreme, and a storm like that can damage any aircraft.
So the Comets kept flying. But it was the first warning.

chapters.name: Lost Over the Sea
sentences: On the tenth of January, nineteen fifty-four, a Comet left Rome on its way to London.
The weather was good. The plane climbed normally over the Mediterranean Sea.
About twenty minutes after takeoff, near the island of Elba, it suddenly broke apart.
The pieces fell into the sea. All thirty-five people on board were killed.
Fishermen near the island saw burning pieces fall from the sky into the water.
There was no storm this time. There was no warning from the pilots. There was no clear reason at all.
The Comets were taken out of service and checked. Engineers made many changes to fix every problem they could imagine.
After about ten weeks, the Comets were allowed to carry passengers again.

chapters.name: It Happens Again
sentences: It took only about two weeks.
On the eighth of April, nineteen fifty-four, another Comet took off from Rome.
It climbed toward its cruising height. Then, near the city of Naples, it fell into the sea.
All twenty-one people on board were killed.
That was three Comets lost in less than a year. Two of them had come apart in clear skies, shortly after leaving the same airport.
Something was wrong with the plane itself. But what?
This time, every Comet was grounded. The most modern airliner in the world was no longer allowed to fly.

chapters.name: The Water Tank
sentences: The British government ordered a full investigation. It was led by a scientist named Sir Arnold Hall.
The navy pulled pieces of the Elba plane up from the bottom of the sea. Slowly, the engineers put the wreck back together, like a giant puzzle.
But Hall's team also tried something that had never been done before on this scale.
They took a complete Comet and built a huge steel tank around its body. Then they filled the tank, and the cabin, with water.
Why water? Because water does not explode the way air does. If the cabin burst, the damage would stay small, and they could see exactly where it began.
Then they pumped the pressure inside the cabin up, and down. Up, and down. Each cycle was like one complete flight.
Day and night, the test Comet flew thousands of flights without ever leaving the ground.
It was slow, patient work. And nobody knew if the answer would ever come.

chapters.name: The Tiny Crack
sentences: On the twenty-fourth of June, nineteen fifty-four, the cabin in the tank burst open.
That plane had made one thousand, two hundred and twenty-one real flights. In the tank, it had lived through one thousand, eight hundred and thirty-six more.
The cause was metal fatigue. Bend a paper clip back and forth enough times, and it snaps. Metal that is loaded again and again grows tiny cracks.
In the wreck pulled from the sea, the investigators found the same thing. A crack had started at a small rivet hole, at the corner of an opening in the roof made for a radio antenna.
At the corners of openings like that, the stress in the metal was far higher than the designers had believed.
After enough flights, a small crack ran through the skin. And the pressure inside the cabin did the rest, in less than a second.
The designers had not been careless. They had tested the cabin to pressures far above normal. But the science of fatigue was still new, and the Comet was the first to fly into it.

chapters.name: The Comeback
sentences: De Havilland redesigned the Comet. The new one had thicker skin and rounded windows, and it was built to stop small cracks from spreading.
It took four years. The new plane was called the Comet Four.
On the fourth of October, nineteen fifty-eight, it began the first regular jet service across the Atlantic Ocean. New York to London took six hours and twelve minutes.
But the world had not waited. Only a few weeks later, the American Boeing seven oh seven started flying the same ocean.
It was bigger. It was faster. And its builders had studied every lesson from the Comet investigation.
Britain's lead was gone. In total, only one hundred and fourteen Comets were ever built.

chapters.name: What It Taught Us
sentences: The Comet Four went on to fly safely for many years. The last Comet flight of all was in March, nineteen ninety-seven.
A military aircraft based on the Comet, called the Nimrod, flew with the Royal Air Force until two thousand eleven.
But the real legacy of the Comet is not a plane. It is knowledge.
Today, every new airliner is tested for fatigue. A full-size airframe is bent and pressurized on the ground, for more flights than it will ever make in its life.
Aircraft structures are designed so that if a crack does begin, it grows slowly, and inspectors can find it in time.
And the idea of rebuilding a wreck piece by piece, to find exactly where a failure began, is now a normal part of air accident investigation.
It is one reason why a modern airliner can safely make tens of thousands of flights.

chapters.name: Outro
sentences: So the next time you look out of an airplane window, look at its shape.
Those smooth, rounded corners are a small reminder of the Comet.
It was the first, so it found the dangers that nobody knew were there. And the people who solved the mystery shared what they learned with the whole world.
That is how flying became so safe. Every hard lesson is studied, written down, and never forgotten.
